Deploying agents requires non-trivial systems design work. Consider a support agent: how do you stream messages to your frontend, how/where do you persist messages for frontend fetching later (or for auditing), and when the agent wants to issue a refund, do you spin-down the compute infra while it's waiting on human approval? Sectr aims to be the serverless abstraction and platform to provide these systems for you.

No sign-up needed to try using the dev server:

  curl -fsSL https://sectr.dev/install.sh | sh # Install CLI
  sectr init my-agent && cd my-agent # Starter code
  sectr dev # Dev server, with UI to test chatting
Sectr provides:

- Streaming of every token, tool call and event, and persistence so they can be loaded fresh later.

- Scaling up, and down to zero when the agent needs to wait, and resumption right to the suspended agent's state.

- Human approved tools automatically use Sectr's suspension and resumption capabilities, no code needed from you.

- AG-UI endpoint for any deployed agent so you can trivially hook up your frontend

- Local dev server experience, so you can rapidly debug and iterate on your agent's behavior

At the core, you can deploy any container image to Sectr as long as it implements a certain shaped HTTP endpoint. In practice, currently Sectr provides adapters to let you deploy your existing OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, or Pydantic AI agents, with only 2 new lines of code:

  app = AgentApp(name="support")
  app.add_route("/chat", openai_agents(agent))
Certainly the hardest part of building Sectr was getting the resumption logic to be correct and invisible, across the Program State x Model Provider x Agent Framework matrix. For example, an earlier bug was when a model replied with text plus a tool call, Sectr would resume that as two separate messages, instead of one message with a text and tool part. This works, but breaks prompt caching (and might subtly change model behavior).

Sectr is free during the beta (and can be tried locally without sign-up); I mainly want feedback, especially on dev & deployment experiences, any bugs, and what features would excite you.

Introductory video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-y3wynkKc0

Its premise is just 12 people sitting in the jury room and sharing their experiences and judgment on a very sensitive case. They need to decide whether a boy is innocent or guilty of a crime.

I have been playing around with a thought experiment where agents play human roles and come to a conclusion. I created agents for each jury, and the judge is another agent that can make an informed decision based on what the juries come up with. I fed the movie script into the setup, and each jury uses the Recall tools to refine their belief, and how they came to a conclusion.

I built this using Polign Recall - https://github.com/Polign/recall , langGraph and agent-sandbox.

1. Each jury agent processes the conversation in its own terms.

2. The memory gets folded, and contradiction and change of mind get processed as part of their own belief system.

3. The judge decides how each juror finally concluded their belief and whether they came to be with an informed decision or were coerced into the decision.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Here is the conclusion by the judge (This is AI generated for a reason) -

As the judge, I'd rule: not guilty, and the verdict stands. The prosecution's case was meant to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and each piece of it fails once tested in the jury room:

The knife isn't unique. Juror 8 bought an identical switchblade in the boy's neighborhood, so the "one of a kind" weapon ties no one to the killing.

The old man couldn't have seen the boy run. He had had a stroke and drags one leg. Walked out in the jury room, he couldn't reach his door in the 15 seconds he claimed.

The woman across the street wasn't wearing her glasses. She had marks on her nose from glasses, and she saw the stabbing from bed, at night, through the windows of a passing train. She wouldn't have been wearing them in bed. "I'm going to kill you" couldn't be heard. The train was passing at that moment, and it's loud enough to drown out speech.

The stab wound doesn't fit. The wound angled downward, but someone experienced with a switchblade stabs underhand. A shorter boy stabbing downward at a taller man is unlikely. The boy forgetting the movie proves little. Juror 3, sitting calmly in the jury room, can't remember a film he saw days earlier.

Did the boy kill his father? Neither the film nor the record answers that, and a judge doesn't rule on it. A judge rules on whether the state proved its case. On this record it didn't: every eyewitness account and every piece of physical evidence fails. Not guilty is the definite answer the evidence supports.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The premise behind the memory updates and storage-

A change of mind is a correction: When a later scene changes what a juror believes, Recall keeps the newer belief as current and keeps the older one as what it replaced, with the scene it came from. A juror who moves from guilty to not guilty carries both beliefs, the scene where each began, and the scene where the first one ended. Recall's diff returns exactly what started and stopped being believed in the final act.

Opinions from memory alone: At the end, each juror is asked what they make of the outcome. The model gets that juror's memory from Recall, and not the script. It answers in the juror's voice and cites the scene behind every belief. If a juror was misled and never found out, they still believe it.

A conclusion from separate minds: The last step reads the final pages and every juror's memory, side by side, and names the question the film leaves open. It answers that question with evidence that names the juror and the remembered scene, for example, a late change of mind, or something one juror knows that another does not. Because each memory was kept apart, the conclusion can see where the jurors disagree."},"title":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"12 Angry Agents"}},"_tags":["story","author_anuptalwalkar","story_50216167","ask_hn"],"author":"anuptalwalkar","created_at":"2026-10-23T22:21:03Z","created_at_i":1792794063,"num_comments":0,"objectID":"50216167","points":1,"story_id":50216167,"story_text":"12 angry men is a very thought-provoking film, and there is nothing quite like it. No supervisor. Just agents, each reacting to their own inputs, coordinating only through shared state. A true leaderless architecture.

They can run kernels, get benchmarks, and even can profile via nsight","title":"Show HN: Agentic CUDA Kernel Optimizer","updated_at":"2026-10-12T22:11:38Z","url":"https://github.com/bertaye/agentic-cuda-optimizer"},{"_highlightResult":{"author":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"jd_"},"story_text":{"fullyHighlighted":false,"matchLevel":"full","matchedWords":["langgraph"],"value":"Hi HN - long-time lurker (since 2012!), first time poster.

Pizza Bot is a self-hosted desktop app for Mac, Windows, and Linux that runs AI agents in the background and exposes them through an email-like UI. Finished work shows up in Unread, and anything waiting on your approval shows up in Action. It's Apache 2.0-licensed, there's no signup and no telemetry, and you bring your own model provider: Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, or a local model through Ollama. There are builds on the releases page, or you can run it from source.

Pizza Bot started as an internal passion project I worked on with a small team at Amazon.

The whole thing came out of my frustration at having to manually log CRM activities through a browser form. I built a simple REST API called "JoeBot" that connected to my authenticated browser session over CDP and filled out the form for me using Playwright. Then I hacked up a quick Obsidian plugin so I could trigger it from my local notes (no AI and no MCP servers involved).

This caught on quickly. My fellow AWS Solutions Architect Igor Fil joined up with me, and we rebranded the project as "Pizza Bot," named after Amazon's two-pizza teams. We started seeing what other automations we could build. We found a GraphQL API we could query and hacked up some "recipes" to pull data out of the CRM to help with meeting prep. That worked great, and it was right around the time MCP servers seemed to be taking off, so we decided to expose Pizza Bot as an MCP server instead, so it would be available to AI tools through natural language.

This was a decent solution for technical users, but the Account Managers who live inside our CRM system wanted something too. We decided to rebuild Pizza Bot as an Electron desktop app modeled after an email inbox, so it would be familiar to non-technical users and would run on both Mac and Windows. We also bundled internal MCP servers as OCI images and hosted them in Amazon ECR as an "addon marketplace" so users could install them with one click without having to set up Amazon developer tooling.

The project took off organically and expanded outside of AWS into the wider Amazon organization globally. More than 2,000 people ended up using it for meeting prep, email drafting, Slack summaries, CRM logging, prioritizing their day, and web research.

Once apps like Claude Cowork and Amazon's own Quick Desktop came out, we realized the real growth opportunity was outside of Amazon. Rather than try to rip out the Amazon-specific integrations, we rebuilt Pizza Bot once more as an open source project. We leaned on coding agents heavily, which is the only reason a team our size could pull off a full rewrite. I'm pleased to say it's finally public, and we're hoping to bring in community members and see where it goes. We'd like to do for knowledge workers what Claude Code and Codex have done for programmers.

A couple of things to know up front. Most of what made Pizza Bot useful on day one inside Amazon came from that internal catalog of skills and MCP servers for Amazon's own systems, and none of it could come out with the app. So it ships thinner than the version those 2,000 people used, and building that catalog back up for tools other people actually use is where we need the most help. It's also a community project and not an AWS service, so there's no support or SLA behind it. The Windows and Linux builds aren't signed yet either.

On the technical side, Pizza Bot is a server and a client. The desktop app bundles both, or you can point a client at a remote backend; personally, I self-host the server on my home network and reach it from my phone over Tailscale. The server owns the thread lifecycle and checkpoints state with DeepAgents and LangGraph, and clients rehydrate from it as needed, so you can disconnect mid-run and pick the thread back up from another client. Approval pauses outlive the session that created them and collect in an Action filter, so you can answer an hour later from a different device. The agent you talk to has a sandboxed QuickJS interpreter that can reach your filesystem only if you grant it a folder, but its main job is to delegate. Each subagent is a 1:1 mapping of a Skill, and an Activity bar shows that subagent and the tool calls it's making as it works. Memory is opt-in and stored as plain markdown files on your machine. Every tool call is explicit, including looking up a memory - we err on the side of transparency to reduce surprises. Tools come from MCP servers, and skills are ordinary SKILL.md files with a per-tool approval policy, so existing skills that don't require a code interpreter should still work.

What I'd most like to hear about is where the app itself gets in your way, the kind of problem you can't fix by writing a skill or an MCP server. I'm around today to answer questions!"},"title":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"Show HN: Pizza Bot – An inbox for AI agents that work in the background"},"url":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"https://github.com/pizza-bot-app/pizza-bot"}},"_tags":["story","author_jd_","story_49713894","show_hn"],"author":"jd_","children":[49720486,49721762,49720073,49721898,49722869,49723174,49768569,49720280,49723294,49720673,49719663,49721286,49720524,49722268,49721569,49722764,49842423,49730330,49726349,49727332,49722670,49726074,49715451,49727979,49713896],"created_at":"2026-09-15T15:20:26Z","created_at_i":1789485626,"num_comments":37,"objectID":"49713894","points":61,"story_id":49713894,"story_text":"Hi HN - long-time lurker (since 2012!), first time poster.

The server owns the thread lifecycle and checkpoints state with DeepAgents and LangGraph, and clients rehydrate from it as needed, so you can disconnect mid-run and pick the thread back up from another client. Approval pauses outlive the session that created them and collect in an Action filter, so you can answer an hour later from a different device. The agent you talk to has a sandboxed QuickJS interpreter that can reach your filesystem only if you grant it a folder, but its main job is to delegate. Each subagent is a 1:1 mapping of a Skill, and an Activity bar shows that subagent and the tool calls it's making as it works. Memory is opt-in and stored as plain markdown files on your machine. Every tool call is explicit, including looking up a memory - we err on the side of transparency to reduce surprises. Tools come from MCP servers, and skills are ordinary SKILL.md files with a per-tool approval policy, so existing skills that don't require a code interpreter should still work.

What I'd most like to hear about is where the app itself gets in your way, the kind of problem you can't fix by writing a skill or an MCP server.
